headline: Skipped Poor Man's, Ran Straight to the Wilmington Elbow — Six Yellowfin, One White Released
subhead: A warm eddy pinched against the canyon wall gave us a hard morning bite before the current went slack and the fish stopped feeding.
body_markdown:
I had two options Wednesday morning and about forty-five minutes to decide between them. Poor Man's had been chattering for a week — small rats mixed with a few respectable yellowfin — but it's crowded water this time of year and the reports were already three days old by the time they hit my ears. Wilmington's eastern wall, up around 38°27'N, 74°09'W where the canyon breaks toward the Sausages, had a cleaner story: a Gulf Stream eddy had pinched in tight against the 100-fathom curve, and the satellite imagery I was working off showed a hard edge instead of a gradual smear. Hard edges concentrate bait. Bait concentrates fish. I ran the extra eight miles.

It paid off, but not the way I'd have scripted it. We started trolling the temp break at first light — naked ballyhoo doubled with a green machine on the shotgun, a small Ilander/ballyhoo combo down the middle, and a spreader bar out back to test the water before committing spread real estate. Inside twenty minutes we had a triple hookup on yellowfin in the 35 to 55-pound class, right where the color changed from that flat green inshore water to a cleaner blue-green push, water reading in the low 70s at the surface — consistent with what the offshore buoys were showing, 72-73°F out past the shelf. That's warm enough to hold yellowfin comfortably and it's exactly the kind of number that makes bigeye stack a little deeper on the same structure, though we didn't get into anything heavier than yellowfin this trip.

The morning bite ran about ninety minutes before the current went from ripping to lazy, and the fish shut off almost like someone flipped a switch. That's canyon fishing in July — the eddy edge is a moving target, and once the tide-driven current relaxes against it, the bait scatters and the tuna stop working the seam. We picked up two more yellowfin working the corner south of the break on a slow troll with cedar plugs before I made the call to switch tactics. Rather than keep burning fuel searching for a bite that had already shut down, we set up to chunk over a hard bottom notch in about 850 feet, butterfish chunks fished on 50-pound fluorocarbon leader, circle hooks, letting the current carry the chunks down without weight. That's where the sixth yellowfin came, and where we had a white marlin come up on a naked ballyhoo skipped just off the flat line — we hooked him, fought him about ten minutes, and released him healthy at the boat. No sail sightings, no wahoo, though the water temp and the bait presence out there suggest wahoo should start showing on the high-speed gear in the next couple weeks if this pattern holds.

Honest assessment: it was a good morning, not a great week. I ran two other trips to Wilmington this week that didn't produce like Wednesday's — one was a troll-only day where we marked plenty of squid on the sounder but couldn't buy a strike, and I suspect the fish had already fed heavy overnight on that bait ball and just weren't interested at 9 a.m. The other trip got blown out early by a building sea state, 2 to 3 foot swell at a short period that made working the spread sloppy, and we came home with one mahi caught incidentally on a rigged ballyhoo near a weed line in about 900 feet. Three trips, one that really produced, two that were work for modest reward. That's a realistic week out here right now — not a bad one, but not the kind where you fill the box without effort.

The bigger picture: squid presence out along the canyon edges this month is a real driver. Shortfin and Illex squid pushing up from the shelf edge are exactly the forage that keeps yellowfin and bigeye holding tight to structure instead of roaming open water, and it's why the bite has been more productive on the hard edges and canyon corners than out in open blue water. If that squid stays put — and there's no strong reason to think it's leaving with water temps sitting where they are — I'd expect the pattern to hold: troll the break at first light while the current's still moving, then be ready to switch to the chunk bag once the tide goes slack and the fish stop chasing.

Looking ahead, if the eddy holds its position against the Wilmington wall through the weekend, I'd run the same corner again — 38°27'N area, working the 100-fathom curve toward the Sausages. If it slides east the way these eddies sometimes do after a few days of current, I'd shift south toward the Baltimore side rather than chase it blind. Either way, I wouldn't leave the dock without both spreads rigged and a chunk bag ready, because right now the fish are telling you when the troll bite ends far more clearly than any weather app will.
